The Modular GTM Team: Specialist Depth Without a Full-Service Agency

By lowob · September 4, 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Strategy / Commercial teams

AI and Web3 companies often need strong specialists for specific periods, without needing every specialist on payroll. A modular GTM team keeps a small group accountable for the strategy and brings in focused support when the work requires it.

AI and Web3 companies often need specialist depth without needing a large permanent team. That gap is becoming an operating model of its own.

Why the usual staffing options fall short

The traditional agency model is built around handing a broad problem to one outside team and expecting an integrated answer.

The freelancer model works the other way. Bring in specialists as needed and manage the system internally.

A lot of AI and Web3 companies fit awkwardly into both.

The mix of work can be unusually broad. A company may need technical positioning, founder content, ecosystem marketing, business development, partnerships, paid distribution, creative, community, events, research, automation, and regional expertise, all sometimes within the same quarter. At the same time, there may not be enough steady volume in any one area to justify building a full in-house function.

So the first problem is often organizational, not tactical.

A large full-service agency can give a company breadth, but breadth alone does not guarantee that the people doing the work are close enough to the commercial problem. The familiar failure mode is that senior people sell the engagement, execution gets split across teams, and the client ends up reconnecting strategy, media, creative, and sales themselves.

A collection of freelancers can produce the opposite problem. The specialists may be excellent, but the company becomes the project manager and integration layer. Someone still has to brief everyone, resolve conflicting recommendations, maintain context, set priorities, manage dependencies, and make the final call.

The senior core keeps the commercial context

The modular GTM model is a practical middle ground.

A small senior core stays close to the business and owns the commercial problem: who the customer is, what the product needs to communicate, what the immediate objective is, which channels matter, how success will be measured, and what should happen next.

Specialists then plug in where there is a real need. That might mean programmatic media, creative, PR, development, automation, data, creator programs, ecosystem research, events, regional execution, or a very specific technical skill.

The model only works if accountability stays clear.

Without someone owning the whole picture, a modular team is just a nicer name for a freelancer roster.

Bring in specialist capacity when the problem changes

That ownership matters especially in markets where the bottleneck changes quickly. One month the issue is positioning. The next is distribution. Then the company needs strategic partners, a launch, a stronger content engine, or a more qualified pipeline. Building a fixed team around every temporary need gets expensive fast.

A modular structure lets the execution layer change without forcing the company to reinvent the commercial strategy every time a new specialist gets involved.

When this model actually fits

This is by no means an argument that full-service agencies are obsolete. They are not. Large agencies make sense when a company needs scale, standardized execution, geographic reach, procurement compatibility, or substantial production capacity.

The more useful question is which operating model matches the actual bottleneck.

If the need is one well-defined function with repeatable volume, hire or retain a specialist. If the company has stable needs across many channels and enough budget to support a large integrated account team, a traditional agency may be the right answer. But when the market, message, and commercial motion are still being worked out, a senior-led modular team can be more efficient and easier to adapt.

AI is pushing this further. Research, first drafts, workflow automation, analysis, prototyping, and creative iteration are all becoming faster and cheaper. That does not remove the need for specialists. It means a smaller senior team can coordinate more work, while context and judgment become even more important.

Media works much the same way. A company may not need a permanent in-house expert for every buying platform, publisher relationship, creator network, region, or campaign type. It does need access to the right operator when the opportunity is real, with one strategy connecting the work.

That is the value of the modular model: specialist depth without carrying the organizational weight all the time.

Keep the commercial thinking close to the business. Bring in specialists when the problem calls for them. Keep one team accountable for the outcome.

For AI and Web3 companies still figuring out exactly how they win, that flexibility can matter more than having every capability permanently on the org chart.

lowob takeaways

  • Keep the commercial problem and outcomes with a named senior owner.
  • Bring in specialists for specific gaps rather than duplicating a full-time organization.
  • A modular team still needs shared briefs, handoffs and clear accountability.
